newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks progress in gas liberalisation talks.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks progress in gas liberalisation talks.

text.p: EU energy ministers will seek to make progress next week in sensitive talks on opening up natural gas markets to more competition but a deal will not be struck until 1997 at the earliest, diplomats said on Friday.

Tuesday's meeting will see the first ministerial debate on a compromise proposal from the Irish presidency designed to narrow the differences between countries pushing for fast and far- reaching liberalisation and those who are more sceptical.
"We can't predict the outcome because we are talking about an issue which is of national importance in a lot of member states," an Irish official said.

The presidency paper -- which has been generally well received -- takes the place of the amended Commission proposal COM(93)643, which was put forward in 1994 but left in abeyance while the EU focused on the twin directive on electricity.

Optimists still hope a deal may be possible during the Dutch presidency in the first half of next year, even if negotiations at civil servant level this autumn have revealed that member states remain far apart on key issues.

"Yes, there are divergent viewpoints on this," one diplomat said. "I'm not sure it will be possible to finalise this during the Dutch presidency...I'm not sure anymore because there is still a lot of work to be done."
For the time being, another diplomat said, there are still some "major discrepancies".
"This dossier will also take some time," he said.
Tuesday's session will focus on four key areas in the fast-growing natural gas market:
-Public service obligations, including how to ensure security of supply.
-The unbundling of accounts to avoid cross-subsidisation.
-Access to the market.
-Take-or-pay contracts, long-term deals which dominate the concentrated European natural gas market.

The Irish proposal incorporates some elements from the EU agreement on electricity liberalisation which ministers reached last June after six years of wrangling, but diplomats stress that there are many differences between the two sectors.
For example, the EU imports a lot of natural gas from potentially unstable countries such as Algeria and Russia.
The market is also less developed, especially in countries such as Greece and Portugal which are just now setting up their gas markets and would need special safeguards.
"They need very careful regimes so that they won't be overrun, they need a planned market," the Irish official said.
In general terms, big producers such as Britain and the Netherlands are enthusiastic liberalisers while France and Belgium are seen as more cautious.
"It is difficult to find a balance in between," one EU official said.
One diplomat noted that Finland and Sweden -- which are traditionally among those countries pushing for liberalisation -- also see themselves as emerging or developing markets.
EU member states remain far apart on issues such as the level of market freedom and how to handle the take or pay deals.
Unlike the agreement on electricity, which foresees a gradual and progressive opening up of national markets, the Irish presidency has proposed a one-off liberalisation for gas.

The proposal uses the same method to calculate the share of the market that would be open to competition as for electricity, including a threshold to determine which consumers will be allowed to shop freely for the best deal.
No figures on the level of market opening have yet been put forward and this looks certain to be a controversial issue.
Germany would like to see EU member states open up their markets completely from the beginning, a position which will not be acceptable to many other member states.
On take-or-pay contracts, those pushing for wide liberalisation believe the Irish proposal goes too far in protecting such deals.
Long-term contracts may create problems in a liberalised environment as purchasers must buy gas at a set price regardless of whether they have a buyer themselves.
Under the presidency proposal on access to markets, member states may choose between two different systems; negotiated or regulated access.
France has so far not pushed for the single buyer solution -- with all contracts between a supplier and a consumer passing through a central buyer -- which was part of the electricity deal.
French industry minister Franck Borotra has said Europe's major concern was to safeguard security of supply, as it depends so heavily on imports.

"We need to avoid emerging competition taking us from a rigid system to an uncontrolled system which could threaten security of supply...France wants to approach deregulation in a different way from the U.S. or U.K.," he said this month.
